title: What is an access token vs refresh token — access token is short-lived for API access; refresh token is long-lived to get a new access token without re-login — and what is refresh token rotation?
shortTitle: Access Token vs Refresh Token and Refresh Token Rotation

s1_definition.profdef: An access token is a short-lived credential (typically minutes) presented on every API call to prove authorization; it is kept small and self-contained so services can validate it statelessly. A refresh token is a long-lived credential (days or weeks) whose only purpose is to obtain a fresh access token from the auth server without forcing the user to log in again; it is kept server-tracked and tightly guarded. Refresh token rotation means each time a refresh token is used, the server issues a brand-new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token becomes detectable and single-use.
s1_definition.analogy: The access token is like a visitor pass at National Bank of India that lets Rajesh move around for only fifteen minutes before it must be renewed. The refresh token is like the master membership card he keeps safely in his wallet; when his short pass expires he shows the membership card at the desk and gets a fresh fifteen-minute pass without signing in again. With rotation, every time he uses the membership card the desk shreds it and hands him a new one — so if a thief copied his old card, the moment either the thief or Rajesh uses it, the bank notices two cards claiming to be the same and locks the account.
s1_definition.oneliner: Short-lived access token for every call, long-lived refresh token to renew it, and rotate the refresh token so theft is single-use and detectable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An access token is a short-lived credential (typically minutes) presented on every API call to prove authorization; it is kept small and self-contained so services can validate it statelessly. A refresh token is a long-lived credential (days or weeks) whose only purpose is to obtain a fresh access token from the auth server without forcing the user to log in again; it is kept server-tracked and tightly guarded. Refresh token rotation means each time a refresh token is used, the server issues a brand-new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a stolen refresh token becomes detectable and single-use.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The access token is like a visitor pass at National Bank of India that lets Rajesh move around for only fifteen minutes before it must be renewed. The refresh token is like the master membership card he keeps safely in his wallet; when his short pass expires he shows the membership card at the desk and gets a fresh fifteen-minute pass without signing in again. With rotation, every time he uses the membership card the desk shreds it and hands him a new one — so if a thief copied his old card, the moment either the thief or Rajesh uses it, the bank notices two cards claiming to be the same and locks the account.

**One line to remember:** Short-lived access token for every call, long-lived refresh token to renew it, and rotate the refresh token so theft is single-use and detectable.

sections.s2_technical:
The access token is sent on each request as `Authorization: Bearer ...` and is validated statelessly by checking signature and expiry. Keeping it short-lived (about 15 minutes) limits the damage window if it leaks. Because it is used constantly, it should not require a database lookup, which is why it stays a self-contained JWT.

The refresh token is used rarely — only when the access token expires — against a dedicated endpoint like `POST /oauth/token` with `grant_type=refresh_token`. Because it is long-lived and powerful, it is stored server-side (hashed) so it can be revoked, and in the browser it belongs in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, never in localStorage. When presented, the server verifies it, then issues a new access token (and, with rotation, a new refresh token).

Refresh token rotation and reuse detection are the senior topics. On each refresh the server stores the new token and marks the old one used. If an already-used (old) refresh token is ever presented again, that signals theft — the server then revokes the entire token family and forces re-login. For example, the server keeps a `refresh_tokens` table with columns for the hashed token, a family id, and a used flag; presenting a used token in a family triggers family-wide revocation. This turns a stolen refresh token into a single-use, quickly-detected event rather than a long-lived master key.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh uses the National Bank of India app all day. If his access token lasted hours and leaked, an attacker would have hours of access; if it lasted only minutes but he had to log in every few minutes, he would be furious. This is exactly why we split tokens — a short access token for safety and a long refresh token for convenience.

Problem 2 — A refresh token is powerful and long-lived, so if one is stolen the attacker could mint access tokens for weeks. This is exactly why rotation exists — each refresh produces a new refresh token and burns the old one, so a stolen token works at most once and its reuse is immediately detected.

Our mini-project builds an `AuthServer` that issues an access/refresh pair, refreshes with rotation, and detects reuse of an old refresh token by revoking the whole family. The demo shows a normal refresh, then simulates a thief reusing the old refresh token and the server locking the family.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run
javac TokenLifecycleDemo.java
java com.bank.lifecycle.TokenLifecycleDemo

# Spring Boot
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/token-lifecycle-service-1.0.0.jar

# Exchange a refresh token for a new access token
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/oauth/token \
  -d 'grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=ref-abc123'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a login for "rajesh", then one normal refresh, then a malicious reuse of the old refresh token.

Step 1: `login("rajesh")` creates a new family id and issues the first pair — a short-lived access token for API calls and a long-lived refresh token stored server-side, marked unused, in that family.

Step 2: `refresh(first.refreshToken)` finds the record, sees it is unused and not revoked, marks it used (burning it), and issues a brand-new pair in the same family. This is rotation — the old refresh token can never be used again.

Step 3: A thief replays the OLD refresh token. The record is now marked used, so presenting it again is treated as reuse. The server revokes the entire family and throws, forcing a full re-login. This converts a stolen refresh token into a single-use, immediately detected event.

Step 4: Even the legitimate second refresh token now fails, because the whole family was locked down when reuse was detected. Rajesh must log in again, which is the safe outcome after suspected theft.

```text
2026-10-31 23:00:00.010 INFO    [TokenLifecycleDemo] Login: access=acc-1a.. refresh=ref-1b..
2026-10-31 23:00:00.012 INFO    [TokenLifecycleDemo] Refreshed: new access=acc-2c.. new refresh=ref-2d..
2026-10-31 23:00:00.013 SEVERE  [TokenLifecycleDemo] REUSE DETECTED: refresh token already used (reuse detected) -> whole family revoked, re-login required
2026-10-31 23:00:00.014 WARNING [TokenLifecycleDemo] Legit token also revoked (family lockdown): refresh token revoked (family locked)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Login(rajesh)
    │
    ▼
  issue pair → access(15m) + refresh(7d, family F, unused)
    │
    ▼  access expires
  refresh(refresh#1)
    │ unused & not revoked
    │ mark refresh#1 USED  → issue access#2 + refresh#2 (family F)
    │
    ├─ NORMAL PATH                     ├─ THEFT PATH
    │  client uses refresh#2 next      │  attacker replays refresh#1 (USED)
    │                                  │  → reuse detected
    ▼                                  ▼
  rotation continues                 revoke ENTIRE family F
                                      refresh#1 AND refresh#2 dead → re-login
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Access + Refresh Token Lifecycle ═══

  ┌────────┐ login/refresh ┌─────────────┐
  │ Client │──────────────→│ Auth Server │ issue pair, rotate, detect reuse
  └────────┘ access(Bearer)└──────┬──────┘
       │                          │ store refresh (hashed) + family
       ▼                          ▼
  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐
  │ Resource API │        │ PostgreSQL   │ refresh_tokens(family,used,revoked)
  │ validate     │        └──────────────┘
  │ access JWT   │
  └──────────────┘
  refresh token stored in HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie on the browser
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — AuthServer token lifecycle ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │          AuthServer          │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ - store: Map<String,         │
  │     RefreshRecord>           │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + login(user): TokenPair     │
  │ + refresh(rt): TokenPair     │  throws TokenReuseException
  │ - issuePair(user,family)     │
  │ - revokeFamily(family)       │
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
                  │ owns ◆
                  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ RefreshRecord {familyId,      │
  │   username, used, revoked}    │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  State of a refresh token:
    ISSUED(unused) ──refresh──→ USED (rotated)
    USED ──presented again──→ REUSE → revokeFamily() → all REVOKED

  Contract for refresh(rt):
    Pre:  rt exists, not used, not revoked
    Post: old rt marked used; new access+refresh returned
    On reuse: revoke whole family, force re-login
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An access token is a short-lived credential, typically about fifteen minutes, that the client sends on every API call to prove authorization, and it is kept small and self-contained so services can validate it statelessly. A refresh token is a long-lived credential, often days or weeks, whose only job is to obtain a new access token from the auth server without forcing the user to log in again. The split gives us both safety and convenience: the constantly-used token has a tiny leak window, while the rarely-used token keeps the user signed in.

In my banking project the mobile app sends the access token on every request and, when it expires, quietly exchanges the refresh token for a new access token in the background, so Rajesh never sees a login screen during the day. The access token is a JWT validated by signature and expiry, while the refresh token is stored server-side in hashed form so we can revoke it, and in the browser it lives in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie rather than localStorage.

Refresh token rotation is the part I emphasize. Every time a refresh token is used, the server issues a brand-new refresh token and marks the old one used, so a given refresh token works at most once. If an already-used refresh token is ever presented again, that is a strong signal of theft, so the server revokes the entire token family and forces a fresh login.

In my demo a normal refresh rotates cleanly, but when a thief replays the old refresh token the server detects reuse and locks the whole family, killing even the legitimate new token until the user re-authenticates. That design turns a stolen refresh token from a long-lived master key into a single-use, quickly-detected incident, which is exactly the guarantee a bank needs.

---

keyPoints: JWT: Header.Payload.Signature — Base64 encoded, not encrypted
Signature verifies integrity — payload is readable by anyone
Access token: short-lived (15 min). Refresh token: long-lived (days)
Store in HttpOnly cookie (XSS-safe), never in localStorage
